work: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition
label: Cells in development minimize surprise and variational free energy like nervous systems
statement: Living systems minimize surprise and optimize variational free energy by tuning internal states to best predict future stimuli, and this holds for individual cells during metazoan development as much as for nervous systems.
quote: Systems minimize surprise and optimize variational free energy by tuning their internal states in a way that optimally predicts future stimuli (Friston and Ao, 2012; Friston, 2013; Badcock et al., 2019). This is as true for nervous systems as it is for individual cells during metazoan development (Friston et al., 2015; Ramstead et al., 2019).
scope: Nervous systems and individual cells in metazoan development

work: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition
label: Multicellularity and morphological complexity are driven by greedy infotaxis
statement: Morphological complexity and multicellularity are proposed to be driven by greedy infotaxis: cells collecting as much information as possible from as far away in space and time as possible to minimize surprise, with greater network connectivity enlarging what the compound individual can sense, remember and store.
quote: It is proposed that morphological complexity and multicellularity are driven by greedy infotaxis (Vergassola et al., 2007) – collecting as much information as possible, from as far away (in both space and time) as possible, to minimize surprise and optimize prediction.
scope: Origin of multicellularity and morphological complexity

work: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition
label: Gap-junction coupling lets cells share sensing and form a larger Self
statement: When cells are coupled into networks by gap junctions, the whole collective can measure and act on the same sensory data, so its Umwelt expands into a larger individual; physiological connectivity is thus the binding mechanism for larger unified Selves.
quote: When coupled into networks via gap junctions however, the whole collective can measure and act upon the same sensory data – the Umwelt expands to create a larger individual in which the comprising cells share a unifying picture of the world (Figure 4).
scope: Gap-junction-coupled cell networks in animal tissues

work: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition
label: Most anesthetics in plants and animals are gap junction uncouplers
statement: Most anesthetics that remove cognition and sensory experience, in both plants and animals, act as gap junctional (bioelectric) uncouplers, which the author takes as consistent with connectivity binding cells into larger Selves.
quote: It is thus no coincidence that most anesthetics used to remove cognition and sensory experience, whether in plants or animals, are gap junctional (bioelectric) uncouplers (Mantz et al., 1993; Wentlandt et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2012; Gremiaux et al., 2014; Baluska et al., 2016).
scope: General and volatile anesthetics used in plants and animals

work: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition
label: Swarms should show the same cognitive illusions as vertebrate brains
statement: The proposed scale-invariant scaling of cognition predicts that swarm organisms should fall prey to the same kinds of cognitive illusions and failures of rationality as vertebrate brains, which the author says has been observed in ants and slime molds.
quote: A prediction of this proposed scaling is that swarm organisms should fall prey to the same kinds of cognitive illusions and specific failures of rationality as do vertebrate brains, which has indeed been observed in ants and slime molds (Sakiyama and Gunji, 2013, 2016; Tani et al., 2014; Beekman and Latty, 2015).
scope: Swarm and collective organisms (ants, slime molds) compared with vertebrate brains

work: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition
label: Selves form only at intermediate levels of information sharing between subunits
statement: Cognitive light cones grow or shrink as an agent's organization changes, and the key is a balance of selective information sharing through "synapses" (any structures that gate signals based on the state of others): too little sharing fails to bind subunits into a new Self, and too much yields an undifferentiated soup without modules or layered abstraction.
quote: Too little sharing results in a failure to bind subunits into a new Self. Too much sharing results in a homogenous soup with insufficient differentiation of modules and abstraction of information across distinct layers.
scope: Multicellular and multi-agent biological systems

work: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition
label: Cancer is a reversible shrinking of a cell's computational boundary
statement: Cancer is a reversible shrinking of the computational boundary of the Self: by becoming isolated from surrounding tissue's physiological (bioelectric) signals, a cell's cognitive boundary shrinks to its pre-multicellular, single-cell size, so it reverts to proliferating and migrating for its own benefit.
quote: Cancer is a (reversible) shrinking of the computational boundary of a biosystem: by isolating itself from the surrounding tissue’s physiological signals, a cell’s cognitive boundary shrinks to the small size it had before multicellularity.
scope: Carcinogenic transformation in metazoan tissues

work: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition
label: Agents scaled up from homeostatic loops by adding memory, anticipation and networks
statement: Agents evolved by scaling up from basic homeostatic loops (whose set points are the first goals), driven by surprise minimization, through the successive addition of delays (memory), anticipation (inference), and spatially distributed networks that allow learning and abstraction.
quote: Agents scaled up by evolving from basic homeostatic loops, driven by active inference (surprise minimization) via addition of delays (memory), anticipation (inference), and networks (spatially-distributed processing that enables learning and progressive abstraction/generalization from data).
scope: Evolution of agency from early living systems to complex organisms

work: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition
label: Morphogenetic goal-directedness smooths the fitness landscape and boosts evolvability
statement: Morphogenetic goal-directedness is a major evolutionary ratchet: because tissues adjust to reach the same anatomical goals despite changed conditions (e.g. muscle, vessels and tendons building a workable extra finger around an ectopic bone), it hides the disruptive effects of random mutations and smooths the anatomical fitness landscape.
quote: Morphogenetic goal-directedness is a major evolutionary ratchet, smoothing the anatomical fitness landscape by hiding the otherwise potentially disruptive effects of random mutations.
scope: Evolution of anatomy in organisms with regulative development

work: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition
label: Brains are not hardwired: ectopic tail eyes in tadpoles still support vision
statement: Brains, like other developing organs, are not hardwired but can ascertain the body's structure and adjust their programs; tadpoles made to develop eyes on their tails, connected to the spinal cord rather than the brain, can still see quite well.
quote: Tadpoles engineered to develop with eyes on their tails instead of in their usual spot can see quite well, despite the fact that the eyes connect to the spinal cord, not the brain (Blackiston and Levin, 2013; Blackiston et al., 2017). Brains, like other developing organs, are not hardwired but are able to ascertain the structure of the body and adjust their functional programs accordingly
scope: Xenopus laevis tadpoles with ectopic eyes; developing nervous systems generally

work: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition
label: Editing bioelectric pattern set points can reprogram anatomy without genome editing
statement: A better strategy for regenerative medicine than genetic rewiring of cells may be to edit the pattern-homeostatic set point and let wild-type cells build to it, as shown by altering bioelectric state in planaria to give permanently double-headed worms without genomic editing.
quote: I have previously suggested that a better strategy than cellular re-wiring at the genetic level may be to edit the pattern-homeostatic set point and let wild-type cells build to the new spec. For example, the ability to re-write target morphology in planarian regeneration was recently shown, by altering the bioelectric state in flatworms, without genomic editing, giving rise to permanently double-headed worms (Durant et al., 2017; Levin et al., 2018).
scope: Regenerative medicine; planarian regeneration as the demonstrating case

work: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition
label: Bioelectric circuits act as software: multistable states switched without genetic change
statement: Ion channel and gap junction circuits are well suited to the "software" of life because they form feedback loops that implement dynamical systems with multiple attractors, which transient signals can switch between without changing the hardware (i.e. without mutating the DNA encoding the channels).
quote: What makes electric circuits, whether ion channel-mediated or electronic, good for software is that they easily implement dynamical systems that have multiple attractors and can be made to occupy one physiological state or another by transient inputs (signals), not requiring changing the hardware (i.e., mutating the DNA encoding that hardware).
scope: Bioelectric networks of ion channels and gap junctions in cells and tissues

work: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition
label: Opiate addictiveness may derive from an ancient role in keeping cells together
statement: If multicellularity arose from a drive to minimize predictive error, cells need a way to keep other cells nearby; this suggests the testable hypothesis that the addictive power of opiates and similar molecules derives from such ancient roots, which could be tested in early models of multicellularity and stem/somatic cell co-cultures.
quote: Specifically, the implementation of multicellularity by the drive to minimize predictive error (Fields and Levin, 2019) suggests that cells need a way to keep other cells nearby. This suggests the testable hypothesis that the addictive power of opiates and similar molecules derives from such ancient roots.
scope: Opioid and addiction-related signalling in early multicellular models and cell co-cultures

work: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition
label: Forced electrogenic and gap junction expression could make unicells form bodies
statement: The proposed role of bioelectrics in multicellularity predicts that forcing expression of appropriate electrogenic proteins and gap junctions in a unicellular organism should induce metazoan-like bodies, and that appropriate changes of bioelectric dynamics may dissolve a metazoan body.
quote: The proposed crucial role of bioelectrics in multicellularity predicts that it should be possible to induce the formation of metazoan-like bodies in an otherwise unicellular organism by forcing the expression of appropriate electrogenic proteins and gap junctions. Similarly, it may be possible to induce dissolution of an entire metazoan body by appropriate changes of bioelectric dynamics.
scope: Unicellular organisms engineered with electrogenic proteins and gap junctions; metazoan bodies

work: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition
label: Regeneration across kingdoms should consistently use electrogenic proteins
statement: Bioelectrics should be widely conserved in regeneration across kingdoms: transcriptomes of regeneration from damaged bacterial biofilms to plants to animal limb and organ regeneration should show consistent use of electrogenic proteins, and neurotransmitter signalling should be conserved enough that cognitive-modulator drugs affect biofilms and Physarum.
quote: Bioelectrics should be widely conserved in regeneration across Kingdoms; transcriptomic analyses of regeneration events from damaged bacterial biofilms to plants to metazoan models of limb and organ regeneration should all show consistent use of electrogenic proteins in the events that enable cooperation toward self-limiting morphogenetic cascades.
scope: Regeneration in bacterial biofilms, plants and animals

work: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition
label: Cells and tissues may have something it is like to make decisions
statement: Because some nervous systems give rise to first-person experience and neural and non-neural networks differ minimally apart from time scale, it is natural to hypothesize that there is something it is like to be a tissue or organ making decisions, e.g. a pancreas may have as much proto-consciousness as a simple neural network.
quote: But, given that at least some nervous systems do give rise to such experience and that the differences between neural networks and non-neural ones (aside from temporal scale) are minimal, it is natural to hypothesize that there is something-it-is-like to being a tissue or organ and making decisions.
scope: Non-neural tissues and organs

work: A scalable pipeline for designing reconfigurable organisms
label: Evolutionary algorithms can design novel living organisms built from frog cells
statement: A pipeline in which an evolutionary algorithm designs candidate organisms in silico for a desired function, and transferable designs are then built from Xenopus cells with a cell-based construction toolkit, can produce novel living systems that show the predicted behaviours, though some steps still need manual intervention.
quote: Here we show a scalable pipeline for creating functional novel lifeforms: AI methods automatically design diverse candidate lifeforms in silico to perform some desired function, and transferable designs are then created using a cell-based construction toolkit to realize living systems with the predicted behaviors.
scope: Xenopus laevis embryonic epidermal and cardiac progenitor tissue shaped into designed aggregates

work: A scalable pipeline for designing reconfigurable organisms
label: Designed organisms moved as simulated when upright, much less when inverted
statement: For at least one deciliated, cardiac-muscle-powered design, the upright organisms' direction of movement matched that of the in silico design under random perturbations, and inverting the design significantly reduced net displacement both in silico and in vivo.
quote: More specifically, the upright organisms’ direction of movement matched that of the in silico design under random perturbations (P < 0.01; details in SI Appendix, section S9), and inverting the design significantly reduced its net displacement both in silico (P < 0.001) and in vivo (P < 0.0001).
scope: Deciliated Xenopus reconfigurable organisms with cardiac tissue, compared with their simulated designs

work: A scalable pipeline for designing reconfigurable organisms
label: Behaviour transfer from simulation to organism was due to the designed shape
statement: The authors interpret the orientation-dependent match between simulated and living organisms as showing that successful transfer of locomotion from simulation to the living organism was due to the designed morphology itself, not chance.
quote: This suggests that successful transference did not result by chance but rather was due to the design itself.
scope: Evolved designs realized as Xenopus reconfigurable organisms

work: A scalable pipeline for designing reconfigurable organisms
label: Motile designs spontaneously aggregate particles in simulation and in vivo
statement: When the environment contains particulate matter, motile designs spontaneously gather the particles into aggregates, both in simulation and as living Xenopus-cell organisms.
quote: When the environment is strewn with particulate matter, motile designs spontaneously aggregate the external objects both in silico (SI Appendix, Fig. S10) and in vivo (Fig. 3F and SI Appendix, Fig. S11).
scope: Xenopus reconfigurable organisms and their simulated counterparts in a particle-strewn dish

work: A scalable pipeline for designing reconfigurable organisms
label: Pairs of organisms collide, bond and orbit, more so with cilia active
statement: Collective behaviours predicted in simulation were observed in vivo: two organisms often collide, form a temporary mechanical bond and orbit each other for several revolutions before detaching, and this is more pronounced when cilia are not inhibited.
quote: For instance, two designs often collide, form a temporary mechanical bond, and orbit about each other for several revolutions before detaching along tangential trajectories (SI Appendix, Fig. S10). This phenomenon is more pronounced when cilia are not inhibited on the organisms
scope: Multiple Xenopus reconfigurable organisms sharing a dish, with and without cilia

work: A scalable pipeline for designing reconfigurable organisms
label: Selection for locomotion under random actuation evolved derandomizing shapes
statement: In the voxel-based soft-body simulation with randomly phased contractile cells, selection for locomotion produced morphologies that derandomize motion: shape and the distribution of passive and contractile cells evolved so the global movement was coherent despite random actuation.
quote: As a side effect of selection pressure for locomotion, derandomizing morphologies evolved: evolutionary improvement occurred through changes in overall shape, and distribution of the passive and contractile cells, to collectively derandomize the global movement produced by the random actuation.
scope: Evolutionary design in a soft-body physics simulation of passive and contractile voxels

work: A scalable pipeline for designing reconfigurable organisms
label: Cell competence lets neural-less novel aggregates self-organize functionally
statement: The behavioural competence of individual cells and their propensity to cooperate in groups facilitate functional morphogenesis in novel circumstances, so that the designed organisms, despite lacking nervous systems, following novel developmental trajectories and mixing tissues, still possess self-organizing properties that support their designed behaviour.
quote: The behavioral competence of individual cells, and the propensity of cells to cooperate in groups, facilitate functional morphogenesis in novel circumstances. The lifeforms presented here, despite lacking nervous systems, following novel developmental trajectories, and being composed of materials from different tissues, nevertheless possess these self-organizing properties.
scope: Xenopus cells in novel, designed multicellular configurations

work: A scalable pipeline for designing reconfigurable organisms
label: Cardiomyocytes in built organisms spontaneously made phase-matched contractions
statement: Although signalling between cardiomyocytes was not designed or enforced, cardiac muscle cells in the built organisms spontaneously coordinated to produce coherent, phase-matched contractions that aided locomotion.
quote: For instance, although signaling between cardiomyocytes was not enforced, emergent spontaneous coordination among the cardiac muscle cells produced coherent, phase-matched contractions which aided locomotion in the physically realized designs.
scope: Xenopus cardiac progenitor tissue embedded in reconfigurable organisms

work: A scalable pipeline for designing reconfigurable organisms
label: Reconfigurable organisms self-repair, closing lacerations
statement: Reconfigurable organisms built from Xenopus cells maintain their externally imposed shape and also self-repair after damage, for example automatically closing lacerations.
quote: Finally, reconfigurable organisms not only self-maintain their externally imposed configuration, but they also self-repair in the face of damage, such as automatically closing lacerations (SI Appendix, Fig. S9).
scope: Xenopus laevis reconfigurable organisms

work: A scalable pipeline for designing reconfigurable organisms
label: Adding hydrodynamics and random actuation made simulated gaits match living ones
statement: Designs first evolved on simulated land had bounding gaits that did not transfer to living organisms; adding first-order hydrodynamics and randomized phase offsets produced designs whose behaviour better matched the living systems, in contact with the ground for 93.3% of evaluation versus 52.7% on the first pass.
quote: The behavior of designs generated on the second pass better matched the behavior of the actual living systems: on average, designs were in contact with the ground plane for 93.3% of their evaluation period, compared to just 52.7% on the first pass (SI Appendix, section S6).
scope: Soft-body voxel simulations of Xenopus reconfigurable organisms

work: A scalable pipeline for designing reconfigurable organisms
label: Shape concavities of 100 µm or more persist in developing stem cell aggregates
statement: Aggregates of developing Xenopus pluripotent cells tend to close small gaps in their geometry; concavities 100 µm wide or more (12% of body length) gave stable long-term deformations, setting the minimal buildable feature size.
quote: Preliminary work determined that concavities with a width of 100 µm or greater (12% of total body length) produced stable long-term deformations suitable for biological building (SI Appendix, Fig. S7).
scope: Reaggregated Xenopus laevis animal-cap tissue shaped by microsurgery

work: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds
label: All known cognitive agents are collective intelligences made of agential parts
statement: Every known cognitive agent is a collective intelligence: biological agents are made of parts (cells and other components) that are themselves agents in important ways, and there is no truly indivisible cognitive being.
quote: All known cognitive agents are collective intelligences, because we are all made of parts; biological agents in particular are not just structurally modular, but made of parts that are themselves agents in important ways.
scope: All known cognitive agents, especially multicellular organisms

work: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds
label: Memories can persist through complete brain regeneration in planaria
statement: In some organisms such as planaria, memories (prior knowledge and behavioural tendencies) can apparently persist after the complete regeneration of the brain, being transferred onto the newly constructed brain.
quote: Not only that, but memories can apparently persist following the complete regeneration of brains in some organisms (McConnell et al., 1959; Corning, 1966; Shomrat and Levin, 2013) such as planaria, in which prior knowledge and behavioral tendencies are somehow transferred onto a newly-constructed brain.
scope: Planarian flatworms trained before decapitation and head regeneration

work: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds
label: Tadpoles with eyes on their tails can still perform visual learning
statement: Xenopus tadpoles engineered to have eyes on their tails instead of their heads are still readily able to perform visual learning tasks, illustrating that minds readily adapt to radically altered body architectures.
quote: When tadpoles are created to have eyes on their tails, instead of their heads, they are still readily able to perform visual learning tasks (Blackiston and Levin, 2013; Blackiston et al., 2017).
scope: Xenopus laevis tadpoles with ectopic eyes transplanted to the tail and native eyes removed

work: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds
label: Transitions in cognitive capacity are gradual, not binary
statement: Although major differences in cognitive function exist among diverse intelligences, transitions between them have not been shown to be binary or rapid relative to the timescale of individual agents; cognition-related properties form a continuum from humble proto-cognitive systems to advanced minds.
quote: Specifically, while major differences in cognitive function of course exist among diverse intelligences, transitions between them have not been shown to be binary or rapid relative to the timescale of individual agents.
scope: All cognitive systems across evolution, development and bioengineered hybrids

work: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds
label: A system's level of agency must be determined empirically by prediction and control
statement: Under TAME, how much agency a system has is an empirical, observer-dependent question: the correct level of agency to attribute is the one whose model and intervention strategy give the most efficient prediction and control of the system, as established by experiment.
quote: Thus, the correct level of agency with which to treat any system must be determined by experiments that reveal which kind of model and strategy provides the most efficient predictive and control capability over the system.
scope: Any living, engineered or hybrid system

work: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds
label: Gene regulatory network models exhibit associative learning
statement: Analyses of biological gene regulatory network models show that they exhibit associative and several other kinds of learning, as well as pattern completion and generalization, suggesting GRNs could be trained with patterned stimuli rather than rewired.
quote: Indeed, recent analyses of biological GRN models reveal that they exhibit associative and several other kinds of learning capacity, as well as pattern completion and generalization (Watson et al., 2010, 2014; Szilagyi et al., 2020; Biswas et al., 2021).
scope: Published ODE models of biological gene regulatory networks

work: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds
label: A Self is marked by goals, compound memories and credit assignment above its parts
statement: TAME defines the hallmarks of a Self as the ability to pursue goals, to own compound (e.g. associative) memories, and to serve as the locus of credit assignment (reward or punishment), each at a scale larger than any of its components can achieve alone.
quote: The TAME framework takes the following as the basic hallmarks of being a Self: the ability to pursue goals, to own compound (e.g., associative) memories, and to serve as the locus for credit assignment (be rewarded or punished), where all of these are at a scale larger than possible for any of its components alone.
scope: Any agent, biological or engineered

work: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds
label: The spatiotemporal scale of an agent's goals delineates its Self (cognitive light cone)
statement: Selves can be classified and compared by the spatio-temporal scale of the goals they can represent and work toward (their 'cognitive light cone'), and this scale delineates the boundaries of each Self.
quote: Specifically (Figure 4), a “space-time” diagram can be created where the spatio-temporal scale of any agent’s goals delineates that Self and its cognitive boundaries.
scope: Agents from microbes to humans and engineered systems

work: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds
label: Stress binds distributed modules into one larger homeostatic loop
statement: Stress, defined as a system-level response to the difference between current state and a setpoint, scales Selves by binding modules that sense and act at different scales and locations into one global homeostatic loop; propagated stress signals recruit distant sub-agents to act so as to reduce their own stress.
quote: Stress is a systemic response to a difference between current state and a desired setpoint; it is an essential component to scaling of Selves because it enables different modules (which sense and act on things at different scales and in distributed locations) to be bound together in one global homeostatic loop (toward a larger purpose).
scope: Multicellular organisms and other multi-scale agents

work: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds
label: Behavioural problem-solving in 3D space derives from older problem-solving in other spaces
statement: Problem-solving behaviour of animals in three-dimensional space is proposed to be a variant of an evolutionarily more ancient capacity to solve problems in metabolic, physiological, transcriptional and morphogenetic spaces.
quote: It is proposed that the traditional problem-solving behavior we see in standard animals in 3D space is just a variant of evolutionarily more ancient capacity to solve problems in metabolic, physiological, transcriptional, and morphogenetic spaces (as one possible sequential timeline along which evolution pivoted some of the same strategies to solve problems in new spaces).
scope: Evolution of problem-solving capacities across life

work: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds
label: Planaria regenerate barium-insensitive heads after barium-induced head loss
statement: Planaria exposed to barium, a non-specific potassium channel blocker, lose their heads but soon regenerate heads that are completely insensitive to barium, by transcriptionally regulating relatively few genes; the authors interpret this as cells navigating transcriptional space to solve a novel physiological stressor not met in evolution.
quote: For example, when planaria are exposed to barium, a non-specific potassium channel blocker, their heads explode. Remarkably, they soon regenerate heads that are completely insensitive to barium (Emmons-Bell et al., 2019).
scope: Planarian flatworms chronically exposed to barium chloride

work: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds
label: Picasso tadpoles with scrambled faces become largely normal frogs
statement: Xenopus tadpoles whose craniofacial organs were placed in abnormal positions ('Picasso tadpoles') tend to become largely normal frogs, because the organs move along novel, abnormal paths and stop at the correct frog-face positions, showing that craniofacial remodelling is goal-directed rather than hardwired.
quote: Amazingly, they tend to turn into largely normal frogs because the craniofacial organs move in novel, abnormal paths [sometimes overshooting and needing to return a bit (Pinet et al., 2019)] and stop when they get to the correct frog face positions.
scope: Xenopus laevis tadpoles with experimentally scrambled craniofacial organs undergoing metamorphosis

work: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds
label: Deer antler trophic memory is a rewritable pattern memory
statement: In deer, a wound made on a branched antler in one year leads to ectopic tines at the same location in later years after the antler is shed, which the author interprets as an experience-dependent, rewritable pattern memory in which the target morphology is rewritten without changing the genome.
quote: This is an example of experience-dependent, re-writable pattern memory, in which the target morphology (the setpoint for anatomical homeostasis) is re-written within standard hardware.
scope: Antlered deer (Cervidae) after antler injury

work: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds
label: Altering planarian voltage patterns changes head number and head species-shape
statement: In planaria, manipulating the endogenous bioelectric voltage pattern by targeting gap junctions or ion channels can produce worms with one, two or zero heads, or with head and brain shapes resembling other extant planarian species.
quote: Manipulation of the normal voltage pattern by targeting the gap junctions (Sordillo and Bargmann, 2021) or ion channels can give rise to planaria with one, two, or 0 heads, or heads with shape (and brain shape) resembling other extant species of planaria (Emmons-Bell et al., 2015; Sullivan et al., 2016).
scope: Regenerating planarian fragments (e.g. Dugesia japonica) treated with gap-junction or ion-channel modulators

work: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds
label: Two-headed planarian state persists through further cutting despite wild-type genome
statement: Planaria with abnormal head number induced by transient bioelectric manipulation are permanently altered: when cut into pieces with no further treatment, the pieces continue to regenerate with abnormal head number despite wild-type genetics.
quote: Remarkably, the worms with abnormal head number are permanently altered to this pattern, despite their wild-type genetics: cut into pieces with no further manipulations, the pieces continue to regenerate with abnormal head number (Oviedo et al., 2010; Durant et al., 2017).
scope: Planarians after transient gap-junction blockade (e.g. octanol) and serial amputation

work: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds
label: Transient bioelectric states can rewrite false pattern memories in animals
statement: Modulating a transient bioelectric state is a conserved mechanism by which false pattern memories (altered target morphologies) can be written into the genetically specified electrical circuits of a living animal, analogous to incepting false behavioural memories in brains with optogenetics.
quote: Thus, much like the optogenetic techniques used to incept false behavioral memories into brains (Vetere et al., 2019), modulation of transient bioelectric state is a conserved mechanism by which false pattern memories can be re-written into the genetically-specified electrical circuits of a living animal.
scope: Regenerating animals, chiefly planaria

work: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds
label: Newt kidney tubules keep correct lumen size when cell size changes
statement: Newt kidney tubules normally made of 8 to 10 cells in cross-section are built from fewer cells when cell size is experimentally enlarged, and from a single cell wrapping around itself when cells are made very large, showing that different molecular mechanisms (cell-cell interactions vs cytoskeletal deformation) can be deployed to reach the same anatomical outcome.
quote: Even more remarkable than the scaling of the cell number to unexpected size changes (on an ontogenetic, not evolutionary, timescale) is the fact that if the cells are made really huge, just one cell wraps around itself and still makes a proper lumen (Figure 6D).
scope: Polyploid newt larvae (Fankhauser's experiments)

work: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds
label: Injury to one limb can be read out from the opposite limb within 30 seconds
statement: Limbs show mirror-neuron-like and somatotopic responses to injury outside the nervous system: the type and site of damage to one limb can be read out within 30 seconds by imaging the opposite, uninjured limb.
quote: For example, mirror neurons and somatotopic representation are seen in limbs’ response to injury, where the type and site of damage to one limb can be read out within 30 s from imaging the opposite, un-injured limbs (Busse et al., 2018).
scope: Xenopus tadpole limbs (Busse et al., 2018)

work: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds
label: Genes for morphogenesis and for learning and memory should overlap widely
statement: TAME predicts significant and specific overlap between genes involved in morphogenesis and genes in memory and learning categories, beyond the known shared ion channels, connexins and neurotransmitter machinery; it also predicts that memory genes will appear in genetic studies of cancer, regeneration and embryogenesis.
quote: Significant and specific overlap are predicted for genes involved in morphogenesis and cognition (categories of memory and learning).
scope: Gene sets across animals, testable by bioinformatics

work: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds
label: Morphogenesis should be trainable by reinforcement for specific anatomical outcomes
statement: TAME predicts (not yet tested) that the collective intelligence of tissues may be trainable by reinforcement learning, using rewards and punishments such as nutrients, endorphins or shock, to produce specific morphological or gene-expression outcomes.
quote: Another key prediction that remains to be tested (ongoing in our lab) is trainability of morphogenesis. The collective intelligence of tissues could be sophisticated enough to be trainable via reinforcement learning for specific morphological outcomes.
scope: Regenerating or developing animal tissues; clinical settings

work: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds
label: Voltage-sensitive channels and gap junctions form rewritable dynamical memories
statement: Because ion channels and gap junctions are themselves voltage-sensitive, a transient voltage state can trigger progressive depolarization or gap-junction closure, so non-neural bioelectric circuits readily form dynamical-system memories that store information and change computation without changing the channel or junction hardware.
quote: The fact that a transient voltage state passing through a cell can set off a cycle of progressive depolarization (like an action potential) or gap junctional (GJ) closure means that such circuits readily form dynamical systems memories which can store different information and change their computational behavior without changing the hardware
scope: Non-neural cell networks coupled by voltage-gated channels and gap junctions

work: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds
label: Gap junctions merge cells into a larger Self by erasing signal ownership
statement: Because signals passing through gap junctions carry no marker of their cell of origin, gap-junctional coupling partially erases informational (memory) boundaries between cells, which promotes the formation of a larger Self whose parts work toward common goals.
quote: Thus, this property of GJ coupling promotes the creation of a larger Self by partially erasing the mnemic boundaries between the parts which might impair their ability to work toward a common goal.
scope: Gap-junction-coupled cell collectives in metazoan tissues

work: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds
label: Cancer is a shrinking of the Self after gap junction closure
statement: Oncogene expression and carcinogen exposure close gap junctions, and the consequence is transformation to cancer, in which cells revert to unicellular-like selves, shrink their computational boundaries and treat the rest of the body as external environment.
quote: Indeed this occurs in cancer, where oncogene expression and carcinogen exposure leads to a closure of GJs (Vine and Bertram, 2002; Leithe et al., 2006). The consequence of this is transformation to cancer, where cells revert to their ancient unicellular selves (Levin, 2021b)—shrinking their computational boundaries and treating the rest of the body as external environment.
scope: Metazoan cells undergoing oncogenic transformation

work: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds
label: Managing bioelectric connectivity induces or suppresses cancer independent of genetics
statement: Managing bioelectric connectivity between cells can override genetically determined states, inducing metastatic melanoma in a wild-type background or suppressing tumorigenesis driven by strong oncogenes such as p53 or KRAS mutations, so genetic alterations are not necessary either to induce or to revert cancer.
quote: Indeed, recent data show that managing this connectivity can override default genetically-determined states, inducing metastatic melanoma in a perfectly wild-type background (Blackiston et al., 2011) or suppressing tumorigenesis induced by strong oncogenes like p53 or KRAS mutations (Chernet and Levin, 2013a,b).
scope: Xenopus laevis embryos (melanocyte conversion and oncogene-induced tumour-like structures)

work: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds
label: Developmental bioelectricity preceded and gave rise to nervous systems
statement: Developmental bioelectrics is an ancient precursor of nervous systems: evolution first used analog bioelectric dynamics to position body configuration in developmental morphospace, long before some cells specialized in fast digital spiking to control behaviour in 3D space.
quote: Evolution first exploited this to enable cell groups to position the body configuration in developmental morphospace, long before some cells specialized to use very fast, digital spiking as neural networks for control of behavior as movement in 3-dimensional space (Fields et al., 2020).
scope: Evolution of bioelectric signalling and nervous systems in animals

work: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds
label: Context-sensitive ion channels appear alongside complex metazoan body plans
statement: Ion channel phylogeny is ancient (many channel families likely predate the most recent unicellular ancestor of animals), and the appearance of context-sensitive channels enabling new bioelectric feedback loops tracks the appearance of complex body plans at the emergence of metazoa, indicating an evolutionary continuum from single-cell excitability to cognition via somatic pattern control.
quote: The phylogeny of ion channels is ancient, and the appearance of context-sensitive channels (enabling new kinds of bioelectrical feedback loops) tracks well with the appearance of complex body plans at the emergence of metazoa (Moran et al., 2015), revealing the remarkable evolutionary continuum that leads from membrane excitability in single cells to cognitive functions in advanced organisms, by way of somatic pattern control (Cook et al., 2014).
scope: Ion channel gene families across unicellular eukaryotes and early-branching metazoans

work: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds
label: A single ion channel can induce complete ectopic eyes where Pax6 cannot
statement: In Xenopus, the action of a single ion channel can induce an eye-specific bioelectric state that creates complete eyes in gut endoderm, spinal cord and posterior tissues, locations where genetic master regulators such as Pax6 are insufficient in vertebrates; bioelectric states thus act as master regulators that evolution can exploit for modular anatomical change.
quote: For example, the action of a single ion channel can induce an eye-specific bioelectric state that creates complete eyes in gut endoderm, spinal cord, and posterior tissues (Pai et al., 2012)—locations where genetic “master regulators” like the Pax6 transcription factor are insufficient in vertebrates (Chow et al., 1999).
scope: Xenopus laevis embryos misexpressing ion channels

work: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds
label: Mutations in electrogenic genes can produce coordinated, long-range anatomical change
statement: Because the same membrane-voltage dynamics can be produced by many ion-channel combinations and bioelectric states act across tissue distances, evolution can swap channels freely, and simple mutations in electrogenic genes can cause long-range, highly coordinated changes in anatomy (supported by KCNH8 and a connexin in an evolutionary shift of fish fin morphology).
quote: evolution is free to swap out channels and explore the bioelectrical state space: simple mutations in electrogenic genes can exert very long-range, highly coordinated changes in anatomy.
scope: Animal morphological evolution, e.g. fish fins

work: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds
label: Multiscale competency shields mutations from selection and smooths fitness landscapes
statement: In organisms with a multiscale competency architecture, whose modules actively correct toward a target morphology, mutations that would be detrimental in hardwired organisms (e.g. displacing the eye) become neutral, so the architecture shields some of mutations' negative effects from selection and smooths the fitness landscape.
quote: Thus, MCA shields from selection some aspects of mutations’ negative effects (which inevitably are the bulk of random mutations’ consequences).
scope: Evolving multicellular organisms; computational models of evolution with competent cells

work: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds
label: Anatomical homeostasis may exist mainly to correct mutation-induced deviations
statement: The primary reason for anatomical homeostasis in regulative development and regeneration may be to correct deviations from target morphology caused by mutations, rather than to repair damage.
quote: The primary reason for the anatomical homeostasis seen in regulative development and regeneration may be for dealing, not with damage, but with deviations from target morphology induced by mutations.
scope: Evolution of regulative development and regeneration in animals

work: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds
label: Systems operating in morphogenetic or transcriptional spaces have minimal consciousness
statement: TAME provisionally holds that consciousness comes in degrees and that embodiment includes perception-action systems in any space, implying that systems operating in morphogenetic, transcriptional and other spaces should have some, if very minimal, degree of consciousness.
quote: This implies, counter to many people’s intuitions, that systems that operate in morphogenetic, transcriptional, and other spaces should also have some (if very minimal) degree of consciousness.
scope: Tissues, cell collectives and other non-neural systems

work: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds
label: General anesthetics block gap junctions, dissolving the higher-level Self
statement: General anesthetics are gap-junction blockers, and on TAME's account shutting down electrical communication between cells makes the higher-level computational layer (the larger Self) disappear while the cells remain healthy; gap-junction blockers anesthetize organisms ranging from plants and Hydra to humans.
quote: Interestingly, general anesthetics are gap junction blockers (Wentlandt et al., 2006): consistent with the cognitive scaling example above, shutting down electrical communication among the cells leads to a disappearance of the higher-level computational layer while the cellular network is disrupted.
scope: Anesthetized plants, Hydra and animals including humans

work: Technological Approach to Mind Everywhere: An Experimentally-Grounded Framework for Understanding Diverse Bodies and Minds
label: Briefly gap-junction-blocked planaria make other species' heads, then revert
statement: Planaria briefly treated with a gap-junction blocker regenerate heads shaped like those of other planarian species but eventually remodel back to their correct species-specific target morphology, which the author takes as parallel to the temporary loss and return of the Self under anesthesia.
quote: Interestingly, and in line with the proposed isomorphism between cognition and morphogenesis, gap junction blockade has exactly this effect in regeneration: planaria briefly treated with GJ blocker regenerate heads of other species, but eventually snap out of it and remodel back to their correct target morphology (Emmons-Bell et al., 2015).
scope: Girardia dorotocephala planarian fragments treated with octanol

work: Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions
label: Published ODE models of gene and protein pathways show several kinds of memory
statement: In simulations of 35 published ODE models of gene regulatory networks and protein/metabolic pathways from BioModels, the networks show several distinct kinds of memory (UCS-based, pairing, transfer, associative and consolidation memory) in response to patterns of node stimulation.
quote: Here, we characterize biological gene regulatory circuit models and protein pathways and find them capable of several different kinds of memory.
scope: 35 ODE pathway models from BioModels (bacteria, slime mould, yeast, plants, vertebrates, mammals)

work: Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions
label: Biological pathway models have more memory than structurally matched random networks
statement: Compared with 500 random gene-circuit networks matched to the biological models in size, edges, degree, betweenness, PageRank and hubness, the biological ODE pathway models show higher prevalence of most memory types, fewer no-memory cases, and more correlated memory types, indicating that generic network dynamics are not solely responsible for trainability.
quote: Random networks do not show similar memory behavior as models of biological processes, indicating that generic network dynamics are not solely responsible for trainability.
scope: 35 BioModels pathway models versus 500 random synthetic gene-circuit ODE models

work: Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions
label: Behaviour-shaping of pathways could be an alternative to gene therapy
statement: Rational stimulation regimes derived from computational models of pathway memory could control pathway function without genomic editing or network rewiring, so behaviour-shaping of pathway responses stands as a potential biomedical alternative to gene therapy (e.g. to counter drug pharmacoresistance and sensitization).
quote: Rational control of dynamic pathway function using stimuli derived from computational models opens the door to empirical studies of proto-cognitive capacities in unconventional embodiments and suggests numerous possible applications in biomedicine, where behavior shaping of pathway responses stand as a potential alternative to gene therapy.
scope: Gene regulatory and protein pathways in cells and tissues

work: Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions
label: Memory is defined functionally as future behaviour modulated by past experience
statement: In the basal cognition framework adopted by Biswas, Clawson and Levin, memory is defined in substrate-independent functionalist terms: a system has memory when its future behaviour is specifically modulated by its past experience, which allows the question of whether molecular networks such as gene regulatory networks are trainable.
quote: Consistent with the basal cognition paradigm, we define memory in functionalist terms—a system in which future behavior is specifically modulated by past experience.
scope: Any system, including gene regulatory networks and protein pathways

work: Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions
label: Nearly all surveyed pathway models have memory; very small networks may not
statement: Memory was found in all but four of the 35 surveyed BioModels pathway models, and three of those four had fewer than four nodes, suggesting that very small networks either cannot have, or are very unlikely to have, memory.
quote: Overall, we found memory models in all surveyed biological networks except four models, of which three had a low number of nodes (<4) suggesting that too small networks either cannot, or are very unlikely to, have memory
scope: 35 ODE pathway models from BioModels

work: Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions
label: No simple network-topology measure predicts memory in pathway models
statement: Across the 35 surveyed BioModels pathway models, the amount of memory showed no significant correlation with mean number of nodes, edges, degree or hubness, so no single network property is indicative of memory.
quote: Additionally, we tested to see if certain network properties, such as mean number of nodes, edges, degree, and hubness were associated with more or less memory and found there were no significant correlations with any of these measures and any memory (see Discussion).
scope: 35 ODE pathway models from BioModels

work: Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions
label: Feedback loops may be conducive to pathway memory but are not the only route
statement: Self-sustaining feedback loops with hysteresis, such as the positive-feedback dual phosphorylation–dephosphorylation cycle of MAPK, may be conducive to memory in biochemical networks, but feedback loop architecture may be only one of many ways to support such memories.
quote: Overall, we suggest that feedback loop network architecture may be conducive to memories but may be only one way of many to support them.
scope: Biochemical reaction networks, e.g. MAPK phosphorylation cycles

work: Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions
label: Pathway memories can form through dynamics alone, without structural change
statement: In ODE models of biological pathways, memories (such as associative memory, in which a neutral stimulus becomes a conditioned stimulus) can be formed by patterns of stimulation through dynamical interactions alone, without changing the network's structure or parameters.
quote: Again, while feedback loop architecture is present, our results indicate that memories can be formed through dynamical interactions alone, without changing network structure/architecture.
scope: ODE models of gene regulatory and protein pathways (e.g. MAPK cascade models)

work: Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions
label: Pathway-model memories are robust to a wide range of stimulus strengths
statement: In the surveyed ODE pathway models, memory formation is robust to training stimuli of 10x, 50x and 100x baseline (most models kept the same number of memories and only 10% lost memories), and some models formed more memories with weaker stimulation.
quote: We conclude that the memory properties are robust to a wide range of stimulus strengths, a desirable property for therapeutics, and also for functional linkages with other cell pathways during evolution.
scope: 35 ODE pathway models from BioModels

work: Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions
label: Noise increases memory in pathway models, especially associative memory
statement: Adding stochastic noise to simulations of the surveyed ODE pathway models left memories intact in most models (83%) and increased memory overall by about 20%, most notably associative memory, suggesting that biological noise does not inhibit and may help the trainability of such networks.
quote: Interestingly, while almost all models retained the memories created (83%), there was an overall 20% increase in memory in the presence of noise (averaged across models and memory phenotypes) most notably in the associative memory paradigm.
scope: 35 ODE pathway models from BioModels with added stochasticity

work: Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions
label: Most pathway-model memories persist over long periods and survive recall
statement: In the surveyed ODE pathway models with UCS-based memory, most networks retain the bulk of their memories over waiting periods up to 100 times the initial one, and testing (recalling) a memory generally does not destroy it and in rare cases strengthens it.
quote: Overall, we conclude that while some networks have a limit on how long they retain training, the majority of networks can retain the bulk of their possible memories over very long time periods and that in general, memory ‘access’ does not destroy the memory but can, in some rare cases, increase memory.
scope: 30 ODE pathway models from BioModels showing UCS-based memory

work: Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions
label: Serially trained associative memories cause catastrophic forgetting in pathway models
statement: When two associative memories are trained one after another in ODE pathway models, all biological and random models show catastrophic forgetting in which both memories are lost, whereas two UCS-based memories can be stored serially or in parallel.
quote: When more complex memories were tested, here AM-AM memory pairs, when created serially all biological and random models showed catastrophic forgetting wherein both are lost.
scope: 35 BioModels pathway models and 35 size-matched random gene-circuit models

work: Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions
label: Pathway memory is distributed uniformly across organism classes
statement: Memory in the surveyed pathway models shows no privileged association with any class of organism (bacteria, slime mould, yeast, plants, lower vertebrates, mammals), being distributed roughly uniformly, which may suggest that proto-cognitive capacity is found across many strata of life.
quote: We found no privileged categorization of memory over classes of organisms—memory seemed distributed uniformly over all strata of life (see Figure S3).
scope: 35 BioModels pathway models grouped by source organism

work: Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions
label: Habituation (pharmacoresistance) occurs in every testable pathway model
statement: Modelling pharmacoresistance as habituation (a progressive 50% drop in response across repeated, lengthening stimulations), at least one habituating stimulus–response pair was found in each of the 27 testable BioModels pathway models, with 1–50% of node pairs per model habituating.
quote: Overall, we were able to test 27 out of the 35 models (77%, see Section 4) and at least one instance of habituation was found for each model, with the distribution of pharmacoresistance across all potential models ranging between 1–50% (see Figure 8 and Figures S11–S13).
scope: 27 ODE pathway models from BioModels

work: Learning in Transcriptional Network Models: Computational Discovery of Pathway-Level Memory and Effective Interventions
label: Pharmacoresistance may be an evolved form of network adaptation
statement: Because random ODE networks rarely show habituation in more than 30% of stimulus–response pairs while biological pathway models differ from that distribution, pharmacoresistance (habituation) may be a form of network adaptation more prevalent in networks shaped by evolutionary pressure, not due to network properties alone.
quote: This would hint that pharmacoresistance may be a form of network adaptation, which would indeed be more prevalent in a biological network shaped by evolutionary pressure.
scope: BioModels pathway models versus 500 random gene-circuit models
